2027-04-04.title: Second Sunday of Easter (Sunday of Divine Mercy)
readings: The whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul
Give thanks to the Lord for he is good, his love is everlasting (or: Alleluia)
Whatever is born of God conquers the world
Christians, to the Paschal Victim offer your thankful praises
A week later Jesus came and stood among them
2027-04-04.alt: Second Sunday of Easter, the Octave Day of Easter, which St John Paul II named for the whole Church the Sunday of Divine Mercy (2000). Gloria and Creed. The Easter Sequence may be sung. The double Alleluia is added to the dismissal today for the last time until Pentecost. A plenary indulgence is granted on this day, under the usual conditions (sacramental confession, Holy Communion, prayer for the intentions of the Holy Father), with a spirit detached from all sin, to those who take part in prayers and devotions in honour of Divine Mercy in any church or chapel, or who pray the Our Father and the Creed before the Blessed Sacrament, adding a devout prayer to the merciful Lord Jesus such as “Merciful Jesus, I trust in you” (Apostolic Penitentiary, 2002). St Isidore (4 April) is not observed this year. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-04.verse: Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.”
theo: Eight days ago the Church sang, “This is the day that the LORD has made.” Today, on the eighth day, the Octave Day of Easter, she sings the same psalm again, and the refrain falls like a drumbeat of mercy: “Let Israel say, ‘His steadfast love endures forever.’ Let the house of Aaron say, ‘His steadfast love endures forever.’ Let those who fear the LORD say, ‘His steadfast love endures forever.’” The first reading shows what that mercy does when it takes hold of a community. “Now the whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one claimed private ownership of any possessions, but everything they owned was held in common.” Luke places at the centre of this picture the preaching of the Resurrection: “With great power the apostles gave their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.” And the fruit is very concrete: “There was not a needy person among them.” Easter faith is not only a conviction in the mind; it opens hands and purses. Mercy received becomes mercy shared.

St John's First Letter tells us where this new life comes from. “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the parent loves the child.” To love God is to love his children, and to keep his commandments, which “are not burdensome.” John then gives one of the great Easter sentences of the New Testament: “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith.” Not our cleverness, not our strength, but faith in the Son of God. Finally John speaks of Jesus as “the one who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ, not with the water only but with the water and the blood.” He is thinking of the Jordan, where Jesus was baptized, and of Calvary, where his side was pierced and “at once blood and water came out” (John 19:34). The Fathers saw in that water and blood the sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist, flowing from the Heart of Christ to give birth to the Church. On this Sunday the newly baptized of Easter night come to the end of their first week in Christ, washed in that water and fed with that Blood.

The Gospel is read on this Sunday every year. It is the evening of Easter Day. The disciples are behind locked doors, “for fear of the Jews,” as John puts it; the disciples were Jews themselves, and John means the Temple authorities who had handed Jesus over, not the Jewish people as such. Into that locked room of fear the Risen Lord comes: “Peace be with you.” He shows them his hands and his side, so that they may know the one who stands before them is the one who was crucified. “Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.” And at once he sends them: “As the Father has sent me, so I send you.” He breathes on them, as God breathed the breath of life into Adam at the creation, and says: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.” On the very first Easter night the Risen Lord gives his Church the power to forgive sins in his name. The Council of Trent taught that in these words Christ instituted the sacrament of Penance. Every confessional is a little upper room where the wounded hands of Christ are raised in absolution and the same words are heard: peace be with you.

Thomas was not there. When the others say, “We have seen the Lord,” he answers with hard words: “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger in the mark of the nails and my hand in his side, I will not believe.” A week later, on the next first day of the week, the disciples are together again and Thomas is with them. Jesus comes, says “Peace be with you,” and turns to Thomas with his own words: “Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.” The Gospel never says that Thomas touched him. It says only that he cried out the greatest confession of faith in all the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!” The doubter becomes the one who names Jesus God. Then the Lord speaks to us, who were not there: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.” In Kerala this Sunday is widely called Puthu Njayar, New Sunday, and many pilgrims climb the hill of Malayattoor, where tradition says St Thomas prayed. And this is why the Church calls it the Sunday of Divine Mercy. The wounds that Thomas was invited to touch are not closed; they have become the open door of mercy. St Faustina saw the Lord with two rays streaming from his Heart, pale and red, the water and the blood, and beneath him the prayer every sinner may make: Jesus, I trust in you. John tells us why he wrote: “so that you may come to believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that through believing you may have life in his name.”
conn: Easter is so great that the Church celebrates it as one day for eight days. Today the Octave ends and the fifty days of the Easter season continue until Pentecost (16 May 2027).

At the canonization of St Faustina Kowalska on 30 April 2000, St John Paul II declared that the Second Sunday of Easter would be called Divine Mercy Sunday throughout the Church. The readings and prayers of the day remain those of the Second Sunday of Easter.
Acts gives three such summaries of the life of the first community (2:42–47; 4:32–35; 5:12–16). Sharing was voluntary and generous, not imposed: Acts 5:4 shows that property remained one's own.

1 John 5:6 recalls Jesus' baptism in the Jordan and his death on the cross, when blood and water flowed from his side (John 19:34). The Fathers saw there the birth of the Church from the side of the new Adam, and the sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist.

In John's Gospel “the Jews” often means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus. Jesus, Mary, the Apostles and the first believers were all Jews; the phrase must never be read as blame on the Jewish people (CCC 597).
The same verb is used in the Greek Old Testament for God breathing life into Adam (Genesis 2:7) and for the breath that raises the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9). Easter evening is a new creation.
The Council of Trent (Session 14, canon 3) taught that by John 20:22–23 Christ instituted the sacrament of Penance, giving the Apostles and their successors the power to forgive and retain sins.

Didymus means “twin.” Earlier Thomas had said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John 11:16), and asked, “Lord, we do not know where you are going” (John 14:5). The tradition of the St Thomas Christians holds that he preached the Gospel in India, arriving at Kodungallur and dying a martyr near Mylapore.
Literally “after eight days.” From the beginning the disciples gathered on the first day of the week, and the Risen Lord met them there. Sunday is the weekly Easter.
altar: The hands and side that Thomas was invited to touch are present on our altar. In the Eucharist we receive the risen, glorified body of the Lord, still marked with the wounds of love. With Thomas we may say in silence at the elevation: My Lord and my God!

The Lord's first word on Easter evening was “Peace be with you,” and his first gift was the forgiveness of sins. Divine Mercy Sunday invites us to come to the altar through the confessional, washed in the mercy that flows from his side.
outline: Ask: what locked room are you sitting in today, and what are you afraid of?
He shows them his hands and side.
The gift of forgiveness on Easter night.

live: If you have not yet made your Easter confession, go this week; if you have, pray for someone who has stayed away for many years.
Say this prayer at three o'clock each afternoon this week, the hour of mercy, or pray the Divine Mercy Chaplet with your family.
At the elevation of the Host and the chalice, say silently: “My Lord and my God.”
Make sure no one is needy
Like the first Christians, share with one family in your parish or neighbourhood that is in real need this month.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (Homily 26 on the Gospels, in substance)

It was not by chance that Thomas was absent. The unbelief of Thomas has done more for our faith than the faith of the disciples who believed; for when he is brought back to faith by touching, our minds are freed from doubt and made firm.
St Augustine (Tractates on John 121, in substance)
He saw and touched the man, and he confessed the God whom he could neither see nor touch. What he saw and touched led him to believe what he could not see.
St John Chrysostom (On the Priesthood 3, in substance)

Priests have received a power that God has given neither to angels nor to archangels. Christ said: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven. What priests do here below, God confirms above; the Master ratifies the sentence of his servants.
St Cyril of Alexandria (On John, in substance)
As in the beginning man was formed from the earth and received the breath of life, so now Christ, renewing our nature, breathes the Holy Spirit upon his disciples. We are created anew.
magis: Even when faced with the reality of the risen Jesus the disciples still doubted; Thomas was brought to faith by the Lord himself.
Only God forgives sins; Christ gave this power to his Apostles and their successors, so that the Church is the place of reconciliation.
On Easter evening the Lord gave the Apostles the Holy Spirit and the power to forgive sins; the sacrament of Penance.
An indulgence is a remission before God of the temporal punishment due to sins whose guilt has already been forgiven.
Dives in Misericordia (St John Paul II, 1980)
The Church lives an authentic life when she professes and proclaims mercy and brings people close to the sources of the Saviour's mercy.
Jesus Christ is the face of the Father's mercy.
saints: Polish religious of the Congregation of the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy (1905–1938). In her Diary she records the Lord's request for an image with the words “Jesus, I trust in you” and for a Feast of Mercy on the Sunday after Easter. Canonized on 30 April 2000; her memorial is on 5 October.
The Twin, whose doubt became the confession “My Lord and my God.” Tradition holds that he brought the Gospel to India. His feast is on 3 July.

5 Apr: the Annunciation of the Lord (transferred from 25 March): Gloria and Creed, with a genuflection at “and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate.” 7 Apr: St John Baptist de la Salle. 11 Apr: Third Sunday of Easter.
2027-04-04.prayer: God of everlasting mercy, who in the very recurrence of the paschal feast kindle the faith of the people you have made your own, increase, we pray, the grace you have bestowed, that all may grasp and rightly understand in what font they have been washed, by whose Spirit they have been reborn, by whose Blood they have been redeemed. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Merciful Jesus, you came through the locked doors of our fear and showed us your wounds. Breathe your Spirit upon us, forgive our sins, heal our doubts, and make us one heart and one soul in your Church. With Thomas we confess you: my Lord and my God. Jesus, I trust in you. Alleluia. Amen.

quick: The first Christians were of one heart and soul, and there was no needy person among them.
Faith in the Son of God is the victory that conquers the world.
The Risen Lord gives peace, the Spirit and the power to forgive sins; Thomas confesses: My Lord and my God.
2027-04-04.action: Pray “Jesus, I trust in you” at three o'clock each afternoon this week, and make your Easter confession if you have not yet done so.
2027-04-04.question: Which locked door in my heart do I need to open to the mercy of the Risen Lord?
catechism: “My Lord and my God”: the title Lord expresses faith in the divinity of Jesus.
Only God forgives sins, and he gives this power to his ministers.
Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, is at the heart of the Church's life.
kidsaint: Helen was a poor girl from a village in Poland who loved Jesus very much. She became a sister and worked in the kitchen and the garden. Jesus showed her a picture of himself with rays of light coming from his heart, and asked her to tell everyone: Jesus, I trust in you! Now that picture is in churches all over the world. Lesson: even when we have done wrong, we can trust in Jesus' mercy.
2027-04-04.special: Second Sunday of Easter, Sunday of Divine Mercy, Octave Day of Easter: Gloria and Creed; Easter Sequence optional; double Alleluia at the dismissal; plenary indulgence under the usual conditions.
term: A remission before God of the temporal punishment due to sins already forgiven, granted by the Church from the treasury of the merits of Christ and the saints (CCC 1471). It is plenary when it removes all such punishment. It presupposes the forgiveness of sins in confession and requires a heart detached from sin.

family.explain: Thomas was not with the others when Jesus came. He said: I will not believe unless I touch his wounds. A week later Jesus came again and said: Thomas, put your finger here. Thomas did not need to touch. He said: My Lord and my God! Jesus said: happy are those who believe without seeing. That means us!
family.intention: We pray for everyone who finds it hard to believe, and for all who need God's forgiveness today.
family.ask: Ask: “When do we say ‘sorry’ in our family?” Then each person says sorry to someone for something small, and the others answer: I forgive you.

illus: An old fisherman in Kollam had not been to confession for nearly forty years. When he was admitted to hospital after a fall, his granddaughter hung a small Divine Mercy picture beside his bed. For two days he pretended not to see it. On the third night he asked her to read the words at the bottom. She read: Jesus, I trust in you. He was quiet for a long time, then said: call the priest. The next morning the hospital chaplain heard his confession. The nurses said afterwards that he slept peacefully for the first time since he came. Mercy had come through a locked door.

pm.open: Merciful Jesus, risen Lord, come into the locked rooms of our hearts, show us your wounds and give us your peace. Jesus, I trust in you. Alleluia. Amen.
share: The whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul (Acts 4:32). What divides our community, and how can mercy heal it?
This is the victory that conquers the world, our faith (1 John 5:4). Where do I need the victory of faith this week?
My Lord and my God! (John 20:28). When did I last speak to Jesus with that kind of faith?
pm.resp: Give thanks to the Lord for he is good, his love is everlasting.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a home of mercy where every sinner finds the open wounds of Christ.
For priests who hear confessions, that they may be patient and gentle ministers of the Father's forgiveness.
For those who doubt, like Thomas, that the Risen Lord may meet them and lead them to faith.
For the poor and needy in our parish, that no one among us may lack what is necessary.
For our group, that we may trust in Jesus and become merciful as the Father is merciful.
pm.close: Father of mercies, by the wounds of your risen Son you have healed us. Make us witnesses of your mercy and one in heart and soul. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, it is evening on the first Easter day, and the disciples are behind locked doors, afraid. Then Jesus comes and stands among them and says: peace be with you (John 20:19). No reproach, no anger, only peace. And he shows them his hands and his side.

Many of us live behind locked doors too: doors of fear, of guilt, of old hurts that we will not let anyone see. The Risen Lord is not stopped by those doors. He comes in, and the first thing he shows us is his wounds, the proof of how much he has loved us.

Then he breathes on them and says: receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them (John 20:22–23). On the very first Easter night Jesus gives his Church the sacrament of mercy. When we go to confession, it is the Risen Lord himself who says through the priest: your sins are forgiven; go in peace.

Thomas was not there, and he would not believe. A week later Jesus comes again, just for him: put your finger here and see my hands. And Thomas cries out: my Lord and my God! (John 20:28). The one who doubted most makes the greatest act of faith. The Lord is patient with our doubts too.

This is why today is called the Sunday of Divine Mercy. Jesus showed St Faustina his Heart, with rays of water and blood flowing out, and asked her to teach the world a simple prayer: Jesus, I trust in you. It is enough to begin there. And mercy, once received, must be shared. The first Christians were of one heart and soul, and there was not a needy person among them (Acts 4:32, 34).

So let us leave this Mass with three things: a heart at peace, because we are forgiven; the words of Thomas on our lips, my Lord and my God; and open hands for the poor. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe. That blessing is for us. Jesus, I trust in you. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, Thomas said: I will not believe unless I touch Jesus' wounds. Then Jesus came and said: Thomas, come and see! And Thomas said: my Lord and my God!
We cannot see Jesus with our eyes, but we believe in him, and Jesus says we are blessed. Let us say together: Jesus, I trust in you!

intro: Peace through the wounds, the Spirit who forgives, the doubter who confesses, and mercy that makes one heart and soul.

sub: Hands and side, the proof of love.
q: But he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed.
After he said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.
points.apply: Bring one fear or old hurt to the Lord in prayer this week and say to him: “Show me your wounds, and give me your peace.”

sub: The breath of the new creation.
Sent as the Father sent him.

If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.

q: The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases, his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
Now the whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one claimed private ownership of any possessions, but everything they owned was held in common.
points.apply: Choose one work of mercy, corporal or spiritual, and do it this week for someone who cannot repay you.

concl: The Risen Lord comes through our locked doors, shows us his wounds and gives us peace and forgiveness.
He leads the doubter to faith and makes his people one in mercy.
2027-04-04.resolve: Pray every afternoon at three this week: “Jesus, I trust in you.”
